chain.g: foot soldier, servant; male commoner; boy

ety.text: From Middle English ladde (“foot soldier, servant; male commoner; boy”), from late Old English *ladda (attested in Old English personal byname Ladda), probably of North Germanic origin. Compare Old Norse ladd (“hose, woolen stocking; sock”), which may have undergone semantic shift to mean a term of abuse (e.g. foolish youth, youngster of lower social status, etc.); thence by connotative amelioration coming to mean any young fellow.

senses.d: A boy or young man.
A hedonistic or irresponsible young man; A Jack the lad.
ex: I think he reckons he’s a bit of a lad.
Last night I was out drinking with the lads.

senses.d: A familiar term of address for a young man.
ex: Come here, lad, and help me shift these boxes.

senses.d: A groom who works with horses.
The penis.
ex: — The lad stood to attention anyhow, he said with a sigh. She's a gamey mare and no mistake.
Just thinking about how she would look without her clothes made his lad twitch with anticipation.

senses.d: A scammer.
ex: [...] regardless whether you feel the lads may deserve to be subjected to those types of images.

grp.label: familiar term of address for a young man
a groom who works with horses

ety.text: Inherited from Middle French garçon, from Old French garçon, garçun m (“servant, boy”), from Early Medieval Latin garciōnem, accusative of garciō m (“mercenary, servant, boy”), from Frankish *wrakkjō (“servant, boy”), from Proto-Germanic *wrakjô (“exile, driven one”).

Inherited from Vulgar Latin *ninnus, probably imitative of infantile language; also could have originated from Latin minimus. Compare also Italian nino and Sicilian nicu. Compare English nun for an English word that is formed similarly from imitative origin of infantile speech, as well as possibly nanny and nana.
Indirectly related to Latin ciccum (“insignificant thing; trifle”); found in several Romance languages as an expressive creation.

Uncertain, probably ultimately identical with muchacho (cf. mocho), or from Latin musteus (“must-like, of new wine, fresh”), from musteum, from mustum. Other theories include a pre-Roman origin. Compare Portuguese moço, Galician mozo, Asturian mozu. Cf. also Catalan mosso (taken from Spanish) and motxo.
From Old Galician-Portuguese rapaz, from Latin rapāx, rapācem (“who robs, plunders”), from rapio (“to grab”).
Inherited from Old French gars, the nominative singular of garçon m, from Early Medieval Latin garciō m.
From older mochacho, from mozo + -acho. Cognate to Portuguese moçaço.

From Caló chavale, from Caló chavó, from Romani ćhavo. Sauraseni Prakrit 𑀙𑀸𑀯 (chāva, “baby animal”), from Sanskrit *छाप (*chāpa). Cognate with Pali chāpa (“the young of an animal”) and Marathi छावा (chāvā, “cub”). Related to Portuguese chavalo and English chav and regional German Chabo.
Probably from Old Occitan palafrenier.

chain.g: mistress of a household, wife of a lord, lady

ety.text: Proto-Indo-European *dʰeyǵʰ-der. Proto-Germanic *daigijǭder. Old English dǣġe Old English hlǣfdīġe Middle English lady English lady From Middle English lady, laddy, lafdi, lavedi, from Old English hlǣfdīġe (“mistress of a household, wife of a lord, lady”, literally “bread-kneader”), from hlāf (“bread, loaf”) + dǣġe (“kneader”), related to Old English dǣġe (“maker of dough”) (whence dey (“dairymaid”)). Compare also lord. More at loaf, dairy, dough. Unrelated to lad.

senses.d: The mistress of a household.
A woman of breeding or higher class, a woman of authority.
ex: "I would like the dining room to be fully set by tonight; would you do so?" "Yes, my lady."

senses.d: The feminine of lord, a lordess.
ex:
’T was the proudest hall in the North Countree,
 And never its gates might opened be,
 Save to lord or lady of high decree[…]

senses.d: A title for someone married to a lord or gentleman.
A title that can be used instead of the formal terms of marchioness, countess, viscountess, or baroness.
A woman: an adult female human.
ex: Please direct this lady to the soft furnishings department.
In Leningrad I met a lady. She was sitting at the hard-currency bar of the Hotel Moscow, sipping gin.

senses.d: A polite reference or form of address to women.
ex: Ladies and gentlemen, it is a pleasure to be here today. Follow me, ladies!

senses.d: Used to address a female.
ex: Hey, lady, move your car!
Hey, ladies, how are you doing?

senses.d: A wife or girlfriend; a sweetheart.
ex:
It is my Lady, O it is my Loue, O that ſhe knew ſhe were,
 She ſpeakes, yet ſhe ſayes nothing, what of that?
But nothing could now exceed my confusion upon seeing the gentleman and his lady enter

senses.d: A woman to whom the particular homage of a knight was paid; a woman to whom one is devoted or bound.
ex:
The ſoldier here his waſted ſtore ſupplies,
 And takes new valor from the Ladies’ eyes.

senses.d: To address as “lady”.
ex: “[…]When I am dead ye’ll mind I said it, my leddy.” “Ah, Elspeth, but do not lady me; say Christine, just wee Christine.[…]”
‘Then, Lady Placida, there is something I wish to ask of you.’ ‘Only,’ she said sternly, ‘if you stop Ladying me. I have a name, dear.’

Inherited from Middle English ladder, laddre; from Old English hlǣder, from Proto-West Germanic *hlaidriju, from Proto-Germanic *hlaidrijō, from Proto-Indo-European *ḱlóydʰrom, from *ḱley- (“to lean”). Compare Scots ledder, North Frisian ladder, Saterland Frisian Laadere, West Frisian ljedder, Dutch ladder, German Leiter; also Old Irish clithar (“hedge”), and Umbrian 𐌊𐌋𐌄𐌈𐌓𐌀𐌌 (kleθram, “stretcher”). See lean, which is related to lid. Further cognates include Ashkun istrī, Kamkata-viri c̣ik, Prasuni čik, čix; Waigali c̣iř, Sanskrit श्रिति (śrití).

senses.d: A frame, usually portable, of wood, metal, or rope, used for ascent and descent, consisting of two side pieces to which are fastened rungs (cross strips or rounds acting as steps).
A series of stages by which one progresses to a better position.
The hierarchy or ranking system within an organization, such as the corporate ladder.
A length of unravelled fabric in a knitted garment, especially in nylon stockings; a run.
ex: You've got a huge ladder in your stockings. I've got a spare pair in my bag, come to the Ladies and you can change.

senses.d: A sequence of moves following a zigzag pattern and ultimately leading to the capture of the attacked stones.
A league table.
To arrange or form into a shape of a ladder.
To ascend (a building, a wall, etc.) using a ladder.
Of a knitted garment: to develop a ladder as a result of a broken thread.
ex: Oh damn it, I've laddered my tights!

senses.d: To close in on a target with successive salvos, increasing or decreasing the shot range as necessary.
ex: Laddering made it possible to get a few hits on a fast-moving, often manoeuvring, target.

senses.d: To corruptly coerce a convicted offender to admit to offences to be taken into consideration which they do not actually believe they committed, as a way to artificially increase the rate of solved crimes.
